Guidelines from the European Society of Radiology (ESR) Abstract The views of the European Society of Radiology concerning what constitutes a good radiological report are outlined in this article. Some pertinent literature is reviewed. Keywords: Radiology report, Quality Aim of the document There is no universally agreed definition of a good radiological report, and both radiologists and those who receive reports may hold differing views on the optimal style and content. Nevertheless, all radiologists wish to produce reports which are accurate and also interpret the investigation for a particular patient in a way that assists with their further management. Medicine is an international subject and, with the advent of picture archiving and communication systems (PACS), images may be transported throughout Europe and indeed the world. Considerable variation currently exists in the way imaging reports are constructed. It can be argued that there is benefit in reducing this variation for ease of comprehension on the part of referrers, and to aid audit, teaching and research. This document suggests a framework, which it is hoped will be relevant to radiological practice throughout Europe. Introduction The written radiological report is the most important means of communication between the radiologist and referring medical doctor [1–3]. It is part of the patient’s permanent health record, and interprets the investigation in the clinical context. The appropriate construction, clarity, and clinical focus of a radiological report are essential to high quality patient care [4]. Knowledge, skills and training required [2] Knowledge 1. Sufficient medical and surgical knowledge to interpret the clinical information provided and understand the suspected underlying pathology 2. Sufficient knowledge to judge the appropriateness of the examination relative to the clinical information provided and other methods of investigation available 3. In-depth knowledge of the accuracy, reliability and potential complications of the investigation 4. Familiarity with the radiological abnormalities shown and with their significance 5. Appreciation of normal variants which may mimic disease 6. An understanding of the relationship between the imaging appearance and the underlying pathology 7. Knowledge of when urgent action is required on the basis of the imaging findings Skills [5] 1. Justification: the ability to make judgements on the clinical justification for the examination 2. Optimisation: the ability to carry out or protocol and optimise the examination 3. Technical: the ability to maximise image and contrast resolution, to minimise exposure to ionizing radiation and to perform relevant image manipulation 4. Observational: the ability to identify radiological abnormalities and distinguish them from normal appearances and variants 5. Image analysis: the ability to evaluate abnormal imaging features and relate them to underlying causative pathology 6. Communication: the ability to convey the interpretation of the investigation clearly, both verbally and in writing, and to communicate directly with the patient where appropriate Training 1. Sufficient training to satisfy local and national regulatory requirements for image interpretation 2. Appropriate training to perform and interpret the particular imaging investigation undertaken Elements of a report Although there are no universally accepted rules for the structure of a radiological report, it can be argued that concise, consistent ordering of the report both reduces variation between reports and makes it easier for referrers who become familiar with the format to assimilate the information [1, 4, 6] The broad categories can be summarised as: * Clinical referral * Technique * Findings * Conclusion * Advice Clinical referral This section should include a brief summary of the reason for referral, summarising the clinical problem. It should be as concise as possible, but should nevertheless contain all the relevant clinical information. It is of the utmost importance that the clinical history of the patient is provided by the referring physician, in order to enable correct image interpretation. If insufficient clinical information is available for the radiologist to give a full interpretation, this should be stated in the report. When appropriate, the justification of radiation exposure should be given. Technique This section should include: 1. A concise description of the investigation/procedure performed, with specific mention of any non-standard elements of the investigation, e.g. additional sequences. 2. All additional medications that were administered to the patient while in the imaging department (e.g. sedatives) should also be recorded. 3. A description of technically suboptimal features if they may have an impact on the accuracy of interpretation. 4. Patient radiation dose where applicable. Findings 1. fetched_contents.text: Insider Guide to Understanding Your Radiology Report Precision and accuracy are crucial in the field of medicine. Radiology reports aid in developing effective diagnostic and treatment strategies tailored to a patient’s specific needs. They’re used to evaluate changes in a patient’s condition. And they help track the effectiveness of therapies. Though primarily intended for referring providers, understanding our radiology report’s basic structure and key terms can help alleviate some confusion. This knowledge can empower us to ask questions and initiate valuable conversations with our doctors. Radiology Report Structure While standardized guidelines exist, radiology reports can differ between institutions based on a facility’s established protocols. For example, certain institutions may incorporate additional sections based on their internal workflows and referring physician preferences. The specific requirements for each subspecialty or imaging modality, such as oncological imaging or mammography, may also vary from practice to practice. These factors often influence the level of detail provided in a report. Some institutions may prefer concise reports focusing on essential findings, while others may include more detailed descriptions or additional information to aid clinical decision-making. A radiologist’s experience and specialty training may also impact the thoroughness of a report. Despite the variability, certain common elements are typically in all radiology reports to ensure clarity and consistency. Understanding the Main Sections in a Radiology Report Radiology reports typically include the following five sections: indication, technique, comparison, findings, and impression. Each serves an essential purpose in communicating the details and results of an imaging procedure. Indication A radiology report’s "indication" section provides a concise description of the clinical reason or suspicion that led to the ordering of the imaging study. It is a communication bridge between the referring healthcare provider and the radiologist interpreting the images. Details typically found in this section include: Patient Information: The patient’s name, age, and gender. Clinical Indication: An outline of any symptoms or specific diagnostic questions the referring physician wants to address through the imaging examination. For example, "lower back pain," "evaluation of a suspected fracture," or "assessment of abdominal mass." Relevant Clinical Findings: In some cases, the indication section may include relevant findings from the patient’s physical examination, laboratory tests, or prior imaging studies. The indication section is crucial for radiologists, as it guides their interpretation and helps them focus on the specific clinical question at hand. By understanding the clinical indication, the radiologist can tailor their analysis and provide a more accurate and relevant report to the referring physician. Technique The technique section in a radiology report typically includes information about the imaging modality used, the specific imaging parameters, and any additional details relevant to the acquisition of the images. Key elements commonly found in the technique section include: Imaging Modality: The imaging technique employed, such as X-ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, or nuclear medicine study. Imaging Protocol: Details of the imaging sequences or the specific views acquired during the study. For example, this section may specify the slice thickness or reconstructions involved in a CT scan. Equipment: Information about the imaging equipment used, including the manufacturer, model, and relevant technical specifications, may be noted. This can be important for quality control. Contrast Administration: If a contrast agent was used during the study, this section outlines the type of contrast (e.g., iodinated contrast, gadolinium-based contrast), the route of administration (intravenous, oral, intra-articular), and the timing of the contrast injection. Limitations: The technique section may mention any limitations or challenges encountered during the study that could affect image quality or diagnostic interpretation. For example, patient motion, obesity, or poor breath-holding. Radiology Report Example: Multiplanar multisequence MR imaging was performed of the brain and IACs with and without contrast. Comparison The "comparison" section in a radiology report provides information about any previous imaging studies available for comparison with the current study. The type of imaging modality (e.g., CT, MRI, X-ray) and the date of the previous study will be specified. This section will also state whether there are any limitations or challenges in comparing the current study with prior images, such as different imaging techniques, incomplete or unavailable prior imaging reports, or significant time gaps between the studies. The comparison section allows the radiologist to provide a more accurate assessment by considering the evolution of findings. It aids in diagnosis, evaluation of treatment response, and identification of new or changing pathology. Additionally, it helps the referring physician understand the significance of any changes in the imaging findings and guides subsequent management decisions. fetched_contents.text: Automated Radiology Report Summarization Using an Open-Source Natural Language Processing Pipeline Abstract Diagnostic radiologists are expected to review and assimilate findings from prior studies when constructing their overall assessment of the current study. Radiology information systems facilitate this process by presenting the radiologist with a subset of prior studies that are more likely to be relevant to the current study, usually by comparing anatomic coverage of both the current and prior studies. It is incumbent on the radiologist to review the full text report and/or images from those prior studies, a process that is time-consuming and confers substantial risk of overlooking a relevant prior study or finding. This risk is compounded when patients have dozens or even hundreds of prior imaging studies. Our goal is to assess the feasibility of natural language processing techniques to automatically extract asserted and negated disease entities from free-text radiology reports as a step towards automated report summarization. We compared automatically extracted disease mentions to a gold-standard set of manual annotations for 50 radiology reports from CT abdomen and pelvis examinations. The automated report summarization pipeline found perfect or overlapping partial matches for 86% of the manually annotated disease mentions (sensitivity 0.86, precision 0.66, accuracy 0.59, F1 score 0.74). The performance of the automated pipeline was good, and the overall accuracy was similar to the interobserver agreement between the two manual annotators. Keywords: NLP, Report summarization, Data extraction, Radiology report Background Radiology reports are a potential treasure trove of data that document the presence or absence, time course, and treatment-response of diseases. They describe in detail the imaging features of specific disease entities and at their best consolidate the varied findings into a concise and coherent impression statement that forms the basis for downstream clinical decision-making. The information in radiology reports exists as free-text and therefore in its raw form is mostly inaccessible to data-mining approaches. A variety of natural language processing (NLP) techniques have been applied to extract data from and classify radiology reports and other clinical texts (reviewed in [1]). Most NLP techniques involve constructing a pipeline or a series of processing steps that are sequentially applied to input text to yield some output. In developing a new NLP technique, it is necessary to manually annotate a set of reports so that the output of the NLP technique can be compared to this “gold-standard” set of manual annotations. Once the NLP technique has been developed and validated in this way, it can then be deployed to process more reports without any further manual annotation required. In the case of a report classifier, those processing steps attempt to divide a collection of reports into a limited set of discrete classes—CT chest reports may be divided into those that assert the presence of acute pulmonary embolism and those that do not, for example, and in this way, the classifier can be used to identify a cohort of patients that share specific clinical characteristics. Report classifiers are generally developed for a specific task, and while they usually perform well at that task, they must be retrained for each separate task (classifying CT head reports on the presence or absence of intracranial hemorrhage or ultrasound abdomen reports on the presence of absence of acute cholecystitis, etc.). In contrast to a report classifier, which takes as its input a free-text report and produces as its output a discrete class assignment for the report as a whole, a data-extraction pipeline takes free-text input and produces structured data as output. The specific data elements and their structure vary depending on the project and are defined upfront by the NLP pipeline developer. These may be project-specific, such as BI-RADS descriptors and categories from mammography reports, or they may be more general, such as all measurements, anatomic site mentions, and disease entities from any report. Most prior work using NLP on radiology reports has focused on extracting a narrow set of features from a limited set of report types. Bozkurt et al. reported high accuracy in extracting lesions and their BI-RADS characteristics from mammography reports [2]. Pham et al. developed a machine learning algorithm that had excellent accuracy to detect thromboembolic disease (DVT and PE) from angiography and venography reports but was considerably less accurate at the more general task of detecting clinically relevant incidental findings [3]. More recently, Hassanpour and Langlotz reported impressive results extracting general features from a diverse report set using a machine learning approach to annotate reports based on an information model capturing anatomy, observations, modifiers, and uncertainty, and determined that this approach is superior to “non-machine learning” approaches [4]. Radiology handoff structure and what the report should include

A radiology handoff should be concise, consistent, and clinically focused, with sections that make the report easier to read and more useful for the receiving provider [N1-F1]. The evidence supports a core structure that includes patient identity, exam details, technique, comparison, findings, and impression, with the impression serving as a concise summary and interpretation of the findings [N1-F2]. For a handoff summary, the most important sections are not just formal headings but the information they carry: patient identity, the clinical indication, the imaging technique used, any comparison with prior studies, and a prioritized account of what was found [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Standard sections such as patient identity and exam details are essential because they anchor the report and help the receiving radiologist understand the context of the study [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that the clinical referral section should be a brief summary of the reason for referral, the clinical problem, and any relevant clinical information, because that guides interpretation and helps the radiologist focus on the specific clinical question [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means including the patient’s identity, date of birth, and the clinical question that prompted the exam, rather than letting those details become buried in a longer report.

Technique is another standard element that should be included because it gives the receiving provider the technical context needed to understand the study’s limitations and relevance [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence says the technique section should include a concise description of the investigation, any non-standard elements, contrast administration, and any limitations that may affect interpretation [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means noting whether the exam was standard or unusual, whether contrast was used, and whether there were technical issues that might have affected the findings.

Comparison with prior imaging is also important because it helps the receiving provider assess changes over time and judge the significance of new findings [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence explicitly says the comparison section should state the type of previous imaging, the date, and any limitations or challenges in comparison [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means briefly noting any prior relevant studies and whether they were available or limited in a way that matters for interpretation.

The essential findings to prioritize are abnormal versus normal findings, and the evidence supports a targeted, systematic, and comprehensive description of abnormalities starting with those relevant to the clinical request or suspected pathology [N1-F1]. The findings section should be precise, using accepted imaging terminology, and should describe dimensions, signal intensity, attenuation, echogenicity, or density where relevant [N1-F1]. In a handoff, abnormal findings should be highlighted first, with enough detail to guide further action but not so much that the summary becomes overly technical. Normal findings may be summarized briefly or omitted unless they are directly relevant to the clinical context.

How to phrase findings in a way that is useful for the receiving radiologist is a key practical point. The evidence emphasizes clarity, precision, and direct communication [N1-F1][N1-F2]. It advises avoiding loose terms such as “shadowing” and instead being specific about what was seen [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means using clear, straightforward language and focusing on the clinically meaningful features that affect management. The impression or conclusion should then be a concise summary and interpretation of the findings, which is especially useful because the evidence says the impression is the final part of the report intended to communicate the overall assessment [N2-F3].

Overall, the handoff should therefore follow a logical structure: patient identity, clinical context, technique, comparison, findings, and impression. For a handoff summary, the report should prioritize abnormal findings, include enough technical and comparative context to support interpretation, and phrase the findings in a way that is concise, precise, and directly helpful to the receiving radiologist [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-F3].

Practical examples and templates for a radiologist's handoff

A radiologist’s handoff should be concise, structured, and focused on the clinically relevant findings, with enough detail to guide the next step without overwhelming the recipient [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F3]. The evidence suggests that a radiologist first dictates the detailed findings and then summarizes the salient findings into a more concise impression or summary [N2-R2]. In a handoff, this means using short, clear phrases that capture the most important abnormalities while omitting unnecessary detail.

Example handoff phrases for common findings should be direct and evidence-based. For an abnormal finding, a good template is: “[Anatomical region] shows [specific abnormality], such as [precise feature], which is [relevant implication or whether further evaluation is needed].” If the finding is normal, the phrase should be equally brief: “[Anatomical region] is normal for the clinical question.” The evidence supports this approach because it emphasizes precise terminology, targeted description, and a conclusion that summarizes the overall assessment [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-F3]. For example, a chest x-ray handoff might say: “Chest x-ray shows no acute pulmonary embolism; no active pleural effusion; no acute fracture; no signs of pneumonia or cardiac enlargement.” In contrast, a finding that needs immediate attention could be stated more urgently: “Left upper lobe mass with possible new consolidation; consider expedited CT scan and infectious workup.”

The evidence also supports avoiding ambiguity and over-interpretation by using accepted imaging terminology and being specific rather than vague [N1-F1]. This means avoiding terms like “shadowing” and instead describing the appearance, location, and any relevant characteristics [N1-F1]. In a handoff, that translates into phrases such as “small left pleural effusion” instead of “a bit of fluid on the left,” or “calcified granuloma” rather than “something old in the lung.” The evidence also says that the impression should be a concise summary and interpretation of the findings [N2-R3], so the handoff should avoid speculation beyond what is supported by the images.

What to omit or simplify in a brief summary is another important point. The evidence suggests that radiology reports should be concise where possible, and that the impression should consolidate the varied findings into a concise and coherent statement [N2-F3]. In a handoff, that means omitting routine technical details that do not affect interpretation, such as the exact sequence parameters unless they are clinically relevant, and simplifying descriptions that are redundant or too detailed for the receiving provider [N1-F1][N2-F3]. For example, instead of listing every minor finding, the handoff should focus on the findings that change management, such as new or worrisome abnormalities, absence of expected findings, or technical limitations that may affect confidence.

Practical templates should therefore follow a simple structure: patient identity, clinical context, technique, comparison, abnormal findings first, and a concise impression or summary. The evidence supports this because it says radiology reports should be concise, consistent, and clinically focused [N1-F1][N1-F2]. In a handoff, the template can be adapted to a few lines rather than a full report, with the impression serving as the final sentence or short paragraph [N2-R3]. An example template is:

- Patient: [Name, DOB]
- Exam: [X-ray, CT, etc.]
- Clinical context: [Indication or suspected pathology]
- Technique: [Brief description and any relevant non-standard elements]
- Comparison: [Prior imaging, if relevant]
- Findings: [Abnormal findings first, then normal or equivocal findings]
- Impression: [Concise summary and next steps, if applicable]

This template helps avoid ambiguity by keeping the language direct and the structure clear, while also allowing the receiving provider to quickly grasp the most important information [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F3].

How to summarize findings for clinical context and next steps

A handoff summary should not just list findings; it should place them in the clinical context and identify the next steps or follow-up exams that are likely needed [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. The evidence supports this because communication failures are common root causes of serious medical errors, and effective handoffs improve shared understanding and reduce errors [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. In a handoff, the receiving provider needs to know not only what was seen but also why it matters and what should be done next.

What clinical context should be included in the handoff summary is a key point. The evidence says communication at the time of the handoff should result in a clear understanding by each clinician about who is responsible for which aspects of the patient’s care [N4-R1]. It also emphasizes that the clinical referral section should be a brief summary of the reason for referral, the clinical problem, and any relevant clinical information [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means including the patient’s identity, the clinical question that prompted the exam, any relevant symptoms, and any prior findings or diagnoses that are relevant to the current interpretation. The evidence further supports that the indication section should include patient information, clinical indication, and relevant clinical findings, because it guides interpretation and helps the radiologist focus on the specific clinical question [N1-F1].

What next steps or follow-up exams are likely needed also depends on the findings and the clinical context. The evidence suggests that handoffs should include an action list and contingency plans, which are central to the I-PASS handoff model [N5-F4]. In a handoff summary, this means explicitly stating whether further imaging is needed, whether a specialist should be consulted, whether medication changes are planned, or whether urgent tests are required. The evidence also says that handoffs are a major communication challenge and that structured handoffs improve communication and patient safety [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. So the handoff should not just state the findings but also specify what the next action is likely to be and who should take it.

When to mention urgency or immediate action is another important part of the summary. The evidence states that communication failures can strongly increase the opportunity for medical errors, and that effective handoff communication is essential to minimize or prevent errors [N4-R1][N4-R3]. In a handoff, any finding that requires rapid attention should be clearly identified. For example, if the findings suggest acute appendicitis, a chest x-ray showing acute pulmonary embolism, or a new mass that needs immediate biopsy, the handoff should explicitly note urgency and the need for expedited action [N4-R1][N5-F4]. The evidence also supports the use of standardized handoff models such as I-PASS, which includes synthesis by the receiver and contingency plans [N5-F4]. This means the handoff should not only tell what was found, but also invite the recipient to confirm understanding and agree on the next steps.

Overall, the handoff summary should be built around the following elements: patient identity, clinical context, findings, and next steps. The evidence supports this because it emphasizes clear communication, shared understanding, and structured action planning [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. In practice, that means including the reason for the exam, any prior relevant findings, and a direct statement of what the next action should be, whether it is another exam, consultation, medication change, or urgent intervention [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Common handoff pitfalls and how to avoid them

The evidence shows that handoffs are a major communication challenge and that incomplete information, ambiguity, and shorthand can lead to misunderstandings and errors [N4-R1][N4-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. One common pitfall is incomplete transfer of information, where important details such as pending test results, medication side effects, or full clinical context are omitted [N6-R5]. Another common pitfall is lack of closed loop communication, which the evidence reports as second most common and associated with 23% of errors [N6-R3]. In a handoff, this means the sender may not confirm that the recipient understood the key points, and the recipient may not be able to ask clarifying questions before action is taken.

A second pitfall is ambiguity or shorthand that can be misunderstood. The evidence says communication failures are common root causes of serious medical errors, and that effective handoffs improve communication and patient safety [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. In radiology, shorthand or vague terms can distort meaning, especially when findings are not described precisely. The evidence also emphasizes that the impression should be a concise summary and interpretation of the findings [N2-R3]. So if a handoff uses imprecise language, such as “some shadowing” or “maybe something,” the receiving provider may misinterpret the significance. The evidence supports avoiding ambiguity by using accepted imaging terminology and being specific [N1-F1]. For example, instead of saying “left lung opacity,” a better phrase is “left upper lobe consolidation,” because it is more specific and easier to act on.

A third pitfall is incomplete transfer, where the handoff does not include all the information needed for safe care. The evidence says handoffs are essential to achieving safe care transitions, and that they are especially common in diagnostic and interventional radiology [N5-R2][N5-R4]. In a radiology handoff, this means the sender should include enough detail so that the recipient can make a confident assessment and decide on the next step. The evidence also supports including the clinical indication, prior imaging, and any relevant findings from the patient’s history [N1-F1]. If those elements are missing, the recipient may misinterpret the findings or fail to recognize a clinically important abnormality.

To avoid ambiguity, shorthand, and incomplete transfer, the evidence recommends using a structured handoff model such as I-PASS, which includes illness severity, patient summary, action list, situational awareness and contingency plans, and synthesis by the receiver [N5-F4]. In a handoff, this means organizing the information in a way that covers the most important aspects and leaves nothing essential to chance. The evidence also says that peer observation with feedback is important for sustaining I-PASS use, which implies that handoffs should be reviewed and refined to ensure they are complete and clear [N5-F4].

What to include instead for clarity and completeness is direct, precise information and a clear action plan. The evidence supports including patient identity, clinical context, findings, and next steps [N1-F1][N4-R1][N5-F4]. In a handoff, that means stating the patient’s identity, the indication or suspected pathology, the findings that matter most, and the next exam or action that should be taken. The evidence also supports using a concise impression that summarizes the overall assessment [N2-R3]. For example, instead of a long run-on paragraph, the handoff can use bullet points or short sentences to separate identity, context, findings, and next steps.

Overall, the common handoff pitfalls are incomplete information, ambiguity, and shorthand, and the evidence shows that structured communication and a clear, concise summary help avoid them [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F4][N6-R3][N6-R5]. A good handoff should be complete, precise, and organized so that the recipient can understand the findings and decide what to do next without needing to ask for clarification later [N1-F1][N2-R3][N5-F4].

## Integrated final answer for the radiologist’s handoff summary

In practice, this means the handoff should be short enough to fit the recipient’s attention span, yet complete enough to guide management.

### 1) What the handoff should include

A good handoff should start with **patient identity**, because that is the anchor for the entire summary [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also says the clinical referral section should be a brief summary of the reason for referral and the clinical problem, because that guides interpretation [N1-F1]. In a handoff for patient #999, that means stating the patient’s name, date of birth, and the clinical question that prompted the x-ray, such as a suspected fracture, infection, or other pathology.

Next, include the **exam and technique** details. The evidence says the technique section should be concise and should describe the imaging performed, any non-standard elements, contrast administration, and any limitations that may affect interpretation [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means noting the modality (e.g., chest x-ray), views or sequences used, contrast if used, and any technical issues that could change how the findings are interpreted.

A **comparison with prior imaging** is important if relevant. The evidence says the comparison section should state the type of previous imaging, the date, and any limitations or challenges in comparison [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means briefly noting whether prior studies were available and whether they were helpful or limited.

Then, the **findings** should be prioritized: abnormal findings first, then normal or equivocal findings. The evidence supports a targeted, systematic, and comprehensive description of abnormalities, starting with those relevant to the clinical request or suspected pathology [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes using accepted imaging terminology and being specific rather than vague [N1-F1]. In a handoff, that means describing the location, appearance, and any relevant characteristics of abnormal findings, while keeping the language direct and actionable.

Finally, the **impression or conclusion** should be a concise summary and interpretation of the findings. The evidence says the impression is the final part of the report intended to communicate the overall assessment [N2-R3]. In a handoff, this means converting the findings into a brief statement that tells the receiving provider what the x-ray shows and what it means for management.

### 2) What to prioritize: abnormal versus normal findings

The evidence explicitly says that the findings section should be precise and that abnormal findings should be highlighted first [N1-F1]. In a handoff, that means starting with the most clinically important abnormalities, such as new masses, fractures, pneumonia, pleural effusion, or other worrisome findings. If the x-ray is normal for the clinical question, that should also be stated clearly, because silence or omission can be as misleading as an incomplete summary [N1-F1].

The evidence also supports using accepted imaging terminology and avoiding vague terms such as “shadowing” [N1-F1]. In a handoff, that translates into specific phrases such as “left upper lobe consolidation,” “small pleural effusion,” or “no acute fracture.” If the finding is normal, the handoff should also say so explicitly, because the absence of expected findings can be meaningful.

### 3) How to phrase findings clearly and concisely

The evidence supports a concise, structured, and clinically focused report [N1-F1][N1-F2]. It also says that a radiologist should first dictate detailed findings and then summarize the salient findings into a more concise impression [N2-R2]. In a handoff, this means using short, direct phrases that capture the most important information.

Example handoff phrases from the evidence are useful:
- “[Anatomical region] shows [specific abnormality], such as [precise feature], which is [relevant implication or whether further evaluation is needed].”
- “[Anatomical region] is normal for the clinical question.”  
- “[Anatomical region] shows no [expected finding].”  
- “[Anatomical region] is equivocal for [differential diagnosis].”  
- “[Anatomical region] appears unchanged from prior study.”  
- “[Anatomical region] is not consistent with [differential diagnosis].” [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-F3]

The evidence also says that the impression should be a concise summary and interpretation of the findings [N2-R3]. In a handoff, this means avoiding speculation beyond what is supported by the images and instead summarizing the overall assessment.

### 4) What to include for clinical context and next steps

The evidence says handoffs should improve communication and reduce errors by creating a shared understanding of responsibility and next steps [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. In a handoff summary, that means including enough clinical context so the recipient can understand why the x-ray matters.

The evidence says the clinical referral section should include the reason for referral, the clinical problem, and any relevant clinical information [N1-F1]. In a handoff for patient #999, that means including the patient’s identity, the clinical question that prompted the exam, and any relevant symptoms, prior findings, or diagnoses that are relevant to the interpretation.

The evidence also supports including an action list and contingency plans as part of a structured handoff [N5-F4]. In practice, that means explicitly stating what follow-up exams are likely needed, whether a specialist should be consulted, whether further tests are required, and whether urgent action is needed.

### 5) When to mention urgency or immediate action

The evidence says communication failures can strongly increase the opportunity for medical errors, and that effective handoff communication is essential to minimize or prevent errors [N4-R1][N4-R3]. In a handoff, any finding that requires rapid attention should be clearly identified.

If the x-ray shows acute findings, such as acute pulmonary embolism, acute appendicitis, or a new mass, the handoff should explicitly note urgency and the need for expedited action [N4-R1][N5-F4]. If the findings are not clearly urgent but still important, the handoff should still state what the next step is, whether it is a follow-up exam, a specialist consult, or a medication change.

### 6) What to omit or simplify in a brief summary

The evidence supports concise reporting and says that radiology reports should be concise where possible, with the impression consolidating the varied findings into a concise and coherent statement [N2-F3]. In a handoff, that means omitting routine technical details that do not affect interpretation, such as exact sequence parameters unless they are clinically relevant, and simplifying descriptions that are redundant or overly detailed.

- Minor technical details that do not affect interpretation.
- Redundant repetition of findings already covered in the impression.
- Vague or imprecise language such as “some shadowing” or “maybe something.”  
- Information that is not directly relevant to the clinical question.

What to keep:
- Patient identity.
- Clinical context.
- Abnormal findings first.
- Normal findings if they are clinically relevant.
- Next steps or follow-up exams.
- Urgency if needed.

### 7) Common handoff pitfalls and how to avoid them

The evidence shows that handoffs are a major communication challenge, and incomplete information, ambiguity, and shorthand can lead to misunderstandings and errors [N4-R1][N4-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. In a handoff, the most common pitfalls are:

To avoid these pitfalls, the evidence recommends using a structured handoff model such as I-PASS, which includes illness severity, patient summary, action list, situational awareness and contingency plans, and synthesis by the receiver [N5-F4]. In a handoff, that means organizing the information in a way that covers the most important aspects and leaves nothing essential to chance.

### 8) What to include instead for clarity and completeness

Instead of vague or incomplete language, the evidence supports direct, precise information and a clear action plan [N1-F1][N4-R1][N5-F4]. In a handoff, that means including:
- Patient identity.
- Clinical context.
- Findings.
- Next steps or follow-up exams.
- Urgency if needed.
- A concise impression that summarizes the overall assessment [N2-R3].

- **Next steps:** [Follow-up exam, consultation, or urgent action, if needed]

### 10) Bottom line

For the radiologist’s handoff summary on patient #999, the evidence supports a concise, clinically focused summary that includes patient identity, clinical context, technique, comparison, abnormal findings first, and a clear impression. The handoff should avoid ambiguity, shorthand, and incomplete transfer by using direct language, specific terminology, and a structured action plan [N1-F1][N2-F3][N4-R1][N5-F4]. ## Integrated final answer for the radiologist’s handoff summary

If a patient asks for a handoff summary for an x-ray done at 10:30 AM on patient #999, the radiologist should provide a concise, clinically focused summary that includes the most important findings, the context that matters, and the next steps. The evidence supports a structured approach: patient identity, clinical context, technique, comparison, findings, and a concise impression or summary [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-F3]. In practice, this means the handoff should be short enough to fit the recipient’s attention span, yet complete enough to guide management.

### 1) What the handoff should include

A good handoff should start with **patient identity**, because that is the anchor for the entire summary [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also says the clinical referral section should be a brief summary of the reason for referral and the clinical problem, because that guides interpretation [N1-F1]. In a handoff for patient #999, that means stating the patient’s name, date of birth, and the clinical question that prompted the x-ray, such as a suspected fracture, infection, or other pathology.

Next, include the **exam and technique** details. The evidence says the technique section should be concise and should describe the imaging performed, any non-standard elements, contrast administration, and any limitations that may affect interpretation [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means noting the modality (e.g., chest x-ray), views or sequences used, contrast if used, and any technical issues that could change how the findings are interpreted.

A **comparison with prior imaging** is important if relevant. The evidence says the comparison section should state the type of previous imaging, the date, and any limitations or challenges in comparison [N1-F1]. In a handoff, this means briefly noting whether prior studies were available and whether they were helpful or limited.

Then, the **findings** should be prioritized: abnormal findings first, then normal or equivocal findings. The evidence supports a targeted, systematic, and comprehensive description of abnormalities, starting with those relevant to the clinical request or suspected pathology [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes using accepted imaging terminology and being specific rather than vague [N1-F1]. In a handoff, that means describing the location, appearance, and any relevant characteristics of abnormal findings, while keeping the language direct and actionable.

Finally, the **impression or conclusion** should be a concise summary and interpretation of the findings. The evidence says the impression is the final part of the report intended to communicate the overall assessment [N2-R3]. In a handoff, this means converting the findings into a brief statement that tells the receiving provider what the x-ray shows and what it means for management.

### 2) What to prioritize: abnormal versus normal findings

The evidence explicitly says that the findings section should be precise and that abnormal findings should be highlighted first [N1-F1]. In a handoff, that means starting with the most clinically important abnormalities, such as new masses, fractures, pneumonia, pleural effusion, or other worrisome findings. If the x-ray is normal for the clinical question, that should also be stated clearly, because silence or omission can be as misleading as an incomplete summary [N1-F1].

The evidence also supports using accepted imaging terminology and avoiding vague terms such as “shadowing” [N1-F1]. In a handoff, that translates into specific phrases such as “left upper lobe consolidation,” “small pleural effusion,” or “no acute fracture.” If the finding is normal, the handoff should also say so explicitly, because the absence of expected findings can be meaningful.

### 3) How to phrase findings clearly and concisely

The evidence supports a concise, structured, and clinically focused report [N1-F1][N1-F2]. It also says that a radiologist should first dictate detailed findings and then summarize the salient findings into a more concise impression [N2-R2]. In a handoff, this means using short, direct phrases that capture the most important information.

Example handoff phrases from the evidence are useful:
- “[Anatomical region] shows [specific abnormality], such as [precise feature], which is [relevant implication or whether further evaluation is needed].”
- “[Anatomical region] is normal for the clinical question.”  
- “[Anatomical region] shows no [expected finding].”  
- “[Anatomical region] is equivocal for [differential diagnosis].”  
- “[Anatomical region] appears unchanged from prior study.”  
- “[Anatomical region] is not consistent with [differential diagnosis].” [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-F3]

The evidence also says that the impression should be a concise summary and interpretation of the findings [N2-R3]. In a handoff, this means avoiding speculation beyond what is supported by the images and instead summarizing the overall assessment.

### 4) What to include for clinical context and next steps

The evidence says handoffs should improve communication and reduce errors by creating a shared understanding of responsibility and next steps [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. In a handoff summary, that means including enough clinical context so the recipient can understand why the x-ray matters.

The evidence says the clinical referral section should include the reason for referral, the clinical problem, and any relevant clinical information [N1-F1]. In a handoff for patient #999, that means including the patient’s identity, the clinical question that prompted the exam, and any relevant symptoms, prior findings, or diagnoses that are relevant to the interpretation.

The evidence also supports including an action list and contingency plans as part of a structured handoff [N5-F4]. In practice, that means explicitly stating what follow-up exams are likely needed, whether a specialist should be consulted, whether further tests are required, and whether urgent action is needed.

### 5) When to mention urgency or immediate action

The evidence says communication failures can strongly increase the opportunity for medical errors, and that effective handoff communication is essential to minimize or prevent errors [N4-R1][N4-R3]. In a handoff, any finding that requires rapid attention should be clearly identified.

If the x-ray shows acute findings, such as acute pulmonary embolism, acute appendicitis, or a new mass, the handoff should explicitly note urgency and the need for expedited action [N4-R1][N5-F4]. If the findings are not clearly urgent but still important, the handoff should still state what the next step is, whether it is a follow-up exam, a specialist consult, or a medication change.

### 6) What to omit or simplify in a brief summary

The evidence supports concise reporting and says that radiology reports should be concise where possible, with the impression consolidating the varied findings into a concise and coherent statement [N2-F3]. In a handoff, that means omitting routine technical details that do not affect interpretation, such as exact sequence parameters unless they are clinically relevant, and simplifying descriptions that are redundant or overly detailed.

What to simplify:
- Minor technical details that do not affect interpretation.
- Redundant repetition of findings already covered in the impression.
- Vague or imprecise language such as “some shadowing” or “maybe something.”  
- Information that is not directly relevant to the clinical question.

What to keep:
- Patient identity.
- Clinical context.
- Abnormal findings first.
- Normal findings if they are clinically relevant.
- Next steps or follow-up exams.
- Urgency if needed.

### 7) Common handoff pitfalls and how to avoid them

The evidence shows that handoffs are a major communication challenge, and incomplete information, ambiguity, and shorthand can lead to misunderstandings and errors [N4-R1][N4-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. In a handoff, the most common pitfalls are:

- **Incomplete transfer**: omitting important details such as pending test results, medication side effects, or full clinical context [N6-R5].
- **Ambiguity and shorthand**: using vague or imprecise language that can be misunderstood [N4-R1][N4-R3][N6-R3].
- **Lack of closed loop communication**: not confirming that the recipient understood the key points, which can lead to 23% of errors in some settings [N6-R3].

To avoid these pitfalls, the evidence recommends using a structured handoff model such as I-PASS, which includes illness severity, patient summary, action list, situational awareness and contingency plans, and synthesis by the receiver [N5-F4]. In a handoff, that means organizing the information in a way that covers the most important aspects and leaves nothing essential to chance.

### 8) What to include instead for clarity and completeness

Instead of vague or incomplete language, the evidence supports direct, precise information and a clear action plan [N1-F1][N4-R1][N5-F4]. In a handoff, that means including:
- Patient identity.
- Clinical context.
- Findings.
- Next steps or follow-up exams.
- Urgency if needed.
- A concise impression that summarizes the overall assessment [N2-R3].

### 9) Practical template for the handoff

A practical handoff template for patient #999 would look like this:

- **Patient:** [Name, DOB]
- **Exam:** [X-ray modality and views, e.g., chest x-ray, lateral, posteroanterior]

  - Abnormal findings: [specific abnormality, location, and relevant features]  
  - Normal findings: [normal for the clinical question, if applicable]  
- **Impression:** [Concise summary and next steps, e.g., “No acute fracture; no active pneumonia; no acute pleural effusion; consider follow-up if symptoms persist.”]  
- **Next steps:** [Follow-up exam, consultation, or urgent action, if needed]

### 10) Bottom line

For the radiologist’s handoff summary on patient #999, the evidence supports a concise, clinically focused summary that includes patient identity, clinical context, technique, comparison, abnormal findings first, and a clear impression. The handoff should avoid ambiguity, shorthand, and incomplete transfer by using direct language, specific terminology, and a structured action plan [N1-F1][N2-F3][N4-R1][N5-F4]. If the x-ray is normal for the clinical question, that should also be stated clearly, because the absence of expected findings can be meaningful [N1-F1].

If the x-ray shows urgent findings, the handoff should explicitly note urgency and the next step [N4-R1][N5-F4]. If the findings are equivocal, the handoff should state that clearly and suggest further evaluation rather than over-interpreting [N1-F1][N2-R3]. Overall, the best handoff is one that is complete, precise, and organized so the receiving provider can understand the findings and decide what to do next without needing to ask for clarification later [N1-F1][N2-F3][N5-F4].
